item.title: How Online Bereavement Therapy Can Assist with the Grieving Process
item.description:
In a disconnected world, there is a new method for navigating grief therapy. Online bereavement has become a new avenue for individuals to navigate the process of losing a loved one. It is a hybrid of traditional mourning and the digital age. People who are grieving frequently face a paradox between needing a community and wanting to grieve alone.

The digital approach of online bereavement offers a lifeline that tailors support to those who have lost a close loved one. It is a place where faith can continue to guide hearts to hope and healing. This modern method acknowledges the evolving ways people can connect. It can also provide a space where emotional wounds can heal, even amid the chaos of loss and daily life.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

Understanding Online Bereavement

Online bereavement involves the grieving process being navigated on digital platforms such as virtual memorials or support groups. Modern life, busy schedules, and the pandemic have changed the way society as a whole grieves. There was a time when we gathered in person to commemorate the passing of loved ones. Now there is a way to share memories online.

Christian counselors can step in and help individuals process the shift to online bereavement so that no one feels as though they are alone in their pain. These counselors bring compassion through their expertise, fostering a sense of belonging in virtual spaces. This can be comforting and transformative for individuals who feel as though they are stranded in the middle of their grief and mourning.

Old grieving methods seem to be ill-fitting in today’s society. This is where online bereavement services adapt and offer forums or video calls for unique losses. This availability allows for grief to be processed so that it does not harden into despair. Though it may be unconventional, this process honors personal pathways and renders the rigid rules of grieving void. It will reveal the layers that accompany any death and meet people where they are with their grief.

Individuals are assured that the flexibility will allow them to express their sorrow at their own pace. Through written tributes or live discussions, a dynamic support network develops, allowing for a separation from traditional support systems.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction… – 2 Corinthians 1:3-4, ESV

The Role of Grief Therapy

Grief therapy is transformed by online bereavement, extending its reach and using virtual sessions to connect those isolated by location or stigma. The cultural message pushes resilience, but online spaces allow raw emotion to surface. The clash between stoic expectations and inner turmoil is resolved, and trauma processing is tailored with care. Christian counselors integrate faith and offer spiritual anchors to those who have lost loved ones.

Professional Christian counselors can provide a steady hand that helps individuals find peace through prayer or scripture. These tools become vital when physical distance separates them from a traditional support system.

This approach breaks barriers and links individuals in rural areas to the support they need. Online bereavement fits into chaotic lives and eases the tension between work and morning. Christian counselors blend scripture with digital tools that prevent individuals from feeling lost in outdated practices.

Technology has enabled counselors to create accessible pathways for healing, ensuring that even the most isolated individuals can find a sense of community. This brings a sense of inclusion and hope, as well as an understanding that they may struggle uniquely, but they are not alone.

Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. – Isaiah 41:10, ESV

Benefits of Seeking Online Healing

The benefits of online bereavement and grief therapy lie in the flexibility of online sessions. Sessions can occur at any time and align with life’s demands. The cultural silence is countered, and vulnerability is allowed to breathe. Privacy draws those hesitant about face-to-face help and creates a haven for them to share their pain. Online groups are also readily available due to the lower costs. This bridges the gap for those who are far from traditional support.

Individuals are empowered through accessibility to seek help on their terms. This reduces the stigma that often comes with public mourning, and it opens doors to healing that may remain closed under traditional grief therapy. Knowing they are in a safe space, individuals who are grieving find freedom and express their emotions, whether positive or negative.

Each of these benefits addresses isolation, enabling people to connect through stories and reducing digital divides and loneliness. It can reduce overwhelming feelings with paced guidance that allows the individual to navigate the grieving process in a way that makes sense to them. Christian counselors use online prayer or Scripture discussions to integrate faith into the healing process. This blend helps individuals avoid feeling adrift.

Christian counselors understand this and can guide individuals through the process with compassion and understanding. The virtual presence of an online counselor offers a consistent source of encouragement. This is beneficial in building resilience over time, a vital component of long-term emotional recovery.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, ESV

Spiritual Integration

Faith can enhance the online bereavement role in grief therapy. Society often splits faith and mental health, creating a conflict in the individual. Scripture is full of hope, and this reframes loss through God’s lens. Online formats connect faith communities for prayer or to understand what Scripture says about grief and hope.

Christian counselors maintain a focus on identity in Christ, which facilitates healing with mercy. Spiritual connection is essential in providing a foundation of strength and resilience. This permits individuals to lean on divine support as a process, which is comforting in the anonymity of online spaces, particularly during their grief.

Journaling and group reflection are virtual tools that root this process in grace. Faith can help prevent isolation and build strength during times of unique loss. A resolution bridges the gap between despair and belief. Christian counselors emphasize the use of spiritual tools to empower individuals during the grief process. By integrating faith and community online, bereavement reminds the individual that they are not walking the path of grief alone.

These tools can encourage deeper exploration of personal faith. This fosters a sense of community and shared purpose that sustains individuals through the darkest moments of their grief journey.

So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. – 2 Corinthians 4:16, ESV

Learn about online grief therapy

Online bereavement assists grief therapy by bridging old and new and challenging the cultural silences of what is acceptable grieving. By transforming solitude into a shared experience, online bereavement challenges the notion that mourning a loss should be a private affair. Individuals emerge transformed in a way that honors the lost loved one.

A faith-based therapy provides enduring comfort and guidance toward a renewed purpose. This transforms grief into a hopeful experience, reminding individuals that even in the midst of loss, they can celebrate the goodness of God. This transformation is a testament to the power of community and faith, leaving a legacy of love that inspires even after the initial pain subsides.

If you would like more information about online bereavement, contact your local Christian counselor today to begin your pathway to healing and connection.

item.title: Hope, Stewardship, and Therapy for Eating Disorders
item.description:
Sometimes our faith, which is meant to bring peace, gets tangled up with harmful eating habits. Spiritual devotion turns into rigid control over food, and we find ourselves trapped in a cycle where discipline becomes disordered eating. This struggle calls for spiritual wisdom and professional care so we can embrace the stewardship of the body God has given us.

Therapy for eating disorders is essential for those of us whose fake journey has been weighed down by restrictive eating and legalistic thinking. This struggle goes beyond the act of simply choosing food. It is created from cultural and religious messages linking spiritual maturity to denying physical means.

Many wrestle with the tension of wanting to honor God through discipline while feeling pressured to neglect our bodies’ needs to prove our faith. This conflict makes our faith feel like a burden and not a blessing. For many of us, the guilt of eating a simple meal can sometimes feel like a betrayal of faith. This is another lie that therapy can help us unravel as we seek to steward our bodies.

Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. – Matthew 4:4, ESV

When Faith Becomes Rules About Food

In our Christian communities, we celebrate virtues such as discipline, self-control, and sacrifice as achievements in spiritual growth. These truths are rooted in scriptures, but we have allowed them to become distorted as we apply them rigidly to our eating habits. We start with practices like fasting in an effort to grow closer to God, only to find ourselves becoming obsessed with controlling our food.

When we turn spiritual practices into a way to earn God’s approval through perfect eating, we run the risk of engaging in self-shame. Fasting is meant to deepen our reliance on God, not to create a pathway of self-punishment. Fasting should never make us feel exhausted or ashamed. This is a mindset based on a false gospel that says worth depends on dietary control, not God’s grace.

We are often caught in a false gospel, where our worth hinges on dietary control, such as our need to feel pure through starvation and avoiding entire food groups. These mindsets only leave us weak and ashamed, facing exhaustion and isolation. Through therapy, we learned to overcome this mindset and realize the way to draw closer to God is to trust His guidance in stewarding our bodies.

Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. – Colossians 2:16, ESV

Breaking Free from Rigid Rules

The similarities between eating disorders and legalistic faith can be striking. Both rely on earning acceptance through strict rule-following, which can create a cycle of striving, failing, and shame. This becomes an exhausting treadmill of always trying to be good enough, but never arriving, and eventually causes problems with mental well-being.

This cycle can be identified by behaviors, such as panic after eating a certain food or weeping because of a fear of failing God for eating a meal. These distorted thoughts reveal the burden that steals the peace of God and leaves us trapped in the false narrative of fasting.

When we pursue this constant effort, we find the peace that God intends for us slipping away. We feel as though we have become trapped, and we question our worth simply because we cannot meet the impossible standards for eating or spirituality. When we experience guilt due to breaking a rule, we tend to set stricter guidelines, creating a harsher cycle of striving and failing. We find ourselves slipping away from resting in grace and into exhaustion from self-punishment.

Christian counselors can offer therapy for eating disorders that will help with recognizing the distorted thoughts surrounding fasting and faith. These counselors help us understand how to build healthier relationships with food in our bodies and how faith can contribute positively. Therapy helps with healing from the struggles by replacing the rigid rules with grace-filled practices.

For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. – Ephesians 2:8-9, ESV

Healing Through Therapy

Choosing to seek therapy is a courageous step that aligns with biblical wisdom. God’s word encourages us to seek counsel and community. Obtaining Christian counseling does not mean there is a lack of trust in God. It can be seen as wisdom leading to the help we need to overcome eating disorders and strict faith rules.

Believers shouldn’t hesitate to seek therapy for fear of judgment. We should allow ourselves to feel freedom as we take a step that breaks down barriers, keeping us from healing through therapy.

Therapy for eating disorders can be complex because they affect thoughts, emotions, and physical health. The care required to treat eating disorders should address biological, psychological, and social factors. Therapy through Christian counselors can provide tools to identify the triggers, challenge harmful thoughts, and rebuild a healthy relationship with food.

Christian counseling provides a unique lens to address how faith can be misused to justify restriction. It also provides direction on how stewardship of the body can support recovery.

When we choose therapy to open doors or deeper spiritual growth, we can address eating disorders and find space to connect with God without shame. Christian counselors can help us reframe things. Biblical truths about stewardship encourage nurturing our bodies and not controlling them.

Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. – Proverbs 11:14, ESV

Reclaiming Body and Soul

Recovering from eating disorders means blending faith and therapy, not choosing one over the other. This recovery is about learning to honor our bodies as God’s temple through stewardship, not punishment. This process will challenge cultural ideas that tie spiritual strength to physical denial. It will require embracing biblical principles for caring for the body.

As we navigate this journey, we will let go of the false security that controlling food provides. It may result in grief over the loss, but true peace will be found in God’s unchanging love. Therapy will help us bridge the gap between knowing God’s grace and living a life surrounded by it. In this journey, we will encounter the unconditional love of God and realize that our actions do not have to earn it. Christian Counseling will help us align our hearts and actions with faith.

Christian counselors promote spiritual practices that support healing. These practices will include gratitude and rest while challenging the distorted use of faith. They will help individuals see their bodies as a gift rather than an enemy that must be conquered.

During the process, we will often realize that the food rules were about controlling our lives, and our restrictive eating may have stemmed from a need to feel worthy. Both of these realizations are ways that distorted thinking creates eating disorders, even when we think we’re being spiritual.

Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body. – 1 Corinthians 6:19-20, ESV

Finding Hope

In the struggle with eating disorders as believers, our freedom will come through seeking spiritual and professional support. We can find practical tools to heal in therapy, while our faith will provide an anchor of identity and worth. Together, these tools bring wholeness, physically, emotionally, and mentally.

As we move forward through the process, we will understand how to let go of false ideas that tie spiritual values to food restriction. We will be able to embrace stewardship, grace, and health as we find a community that supports our healing journey.

This journey is about finding God’s promise of healing as we seek it through every means He has provided. Call your local Christian counselor to start your journey of freedom from disordered eating to discover hope!

item.title: School-Based Social Emotional Learning and Mental Health for Teens
item.description:
Parents and educators are realizing that there is a rise in the number of teens experiencing anxiety and depression. Many teens wrestle with emotions they can’t quite name. Schools have become more than places for academic learning. They are now spaces where adolescents’ mental health is addressed through structured programs.

These programs are teaching skills that their parents were never taught in classrooms. Social-emotional learning has become a response to the growing need for mental health support among adolescents. As these programs expand, they raise questions about their purpose, place in the curriculum, and role in schools.

Social-emotional learning programs are built on self-awareness, self-management, relationship skills, responsible decision-making, and social awareness. These concepts aren’t new to navigating life. They are skills we have always needed to navigate life well.

There is now an intentional focus on teaching these skills in schools. The goal is universal support for all students. The idea is straightforward: if adolescents can identify their emotions, manage stress, understand others’ perspectives, build healthy relationships, and make thoughtful decisions, they’ll be better equipped than we were at their age.

Schools with social-emotional learning programs are showing improved academic performance and stronger emotional well-being among their students.

Understanding What Social Emotional Learning Actually Teaches

Students in schools with social-emotional learning curricula develop skills that begin in early childhood and continue throughout adolescence. Self-awareness teaches students to recognize emotions and understand how their feelings influence their behavior. It is a foundation for everything else.

Teens who can identify anxiety before a test have information to work with. Self-management provides a strategy for regulating emotions and working toward goals, even when stress feels overwhelming. The practical approaches taught in these programs, like deep breathing, positive self-talk, and breaking tasks into manageable steps, help students navigate those moments of high anxiety and stress.

The social awareness aspect of this learning program focuses on developing empathy and understanding perspectives. This competency aims to bridge cultural and social differences and to develop relationship skills for communication, active listening, and conflict resolution.

Responsible decision-making encourages teens to consider consequences, evaluate options, and make choices aligned with their core values. These competencies address the real needs of adolescents facing academic pressure, social media, social comparison, uncertainty about the future, and complex social dynamics that previous generations never encountered.

The question is not whether the skills matter. The question is whether schools are the appropriate venue for teaching them and whether these programs align with the values parents seek to instill at home.

The Gap Between Program Goals and Mental Health for Teens

When it comes to program goals and mental health for teens, the conversation gets complicated. Social and emotional learning programs have good intentions, but implementation can vary across schools and districts. Questions about integrating these competencies into the existing curriculum reveal gaps between goals and actual implementation.

Teachers incorporate discussions of emotions and relationships into lessons, activities, and group projects. Some schools dedicate time to social-emotional learning and treat it as a separate subject. Other schools approach it through discipline and classroom management strategies. This inconsistency creates confusion for parents seeking to understand the adolescents’ social-emotional learning.

The biggest concern is the gap between what these programs promise and what teens actually need when it comes to mental health awareness. Teaching a teenager to identify emotions and manage stress sounds helpful, but it does not address the deeper issues that drive anxiety and depression rates to such high levels.

A program that teaches deep-breathing techniques doesn’t address the underlying pressure that adolescents feel to perform academically or to present a perfect image on social media. Christian counselors who are trained in mental health for teens frequently see a disconnect between the program and what teens are actually learning about mental health.

These teens come into counseling understanding the language of emotional intelligence, but with none of the tools to address the unresolved trauma, fractured relationships, or spiritual emptiness. They know how to name their feelings but do not know how to act on them in a meaningful and productive way.

The Intersection of Faith and Emotional Development

The Christian perspective on emotional development begins with a different foundation. Scripture teaches us that we are created in God’s image, fearfully and wonderfully made, with an inherent worth that doesn’t depend on performance.

We approach emotional struggles on the basis of this truth. We don’t view anxiety as simply a skill deficit needing better coping strategies. Our faith acknowledges that some distress comes from living in a broken world.

This doesn’t mean we dismiss practical skills for understanding our emotions. However, it indicates that we learn to manage emotions, understand others, and make wise choices by following biblical principles grounded in something more profound than self-improvement.

When Christian counselors integrate faith and therapeutic approaches to support the mental health of teens, they are addressing the whole person. This approach teaches teens that self-awareness includes understanding their identity in Christ, not just recognizing their emotions. Self-management is not merely about willpower but also about understanding how to rely on God’s strength.

Through faith, they learn that social awareness flows from seeing others as image bearers, worthy of respect and compassion. They also understand that relationship skills are built on biblical principles of love, forgiveness, and grace, and that God’s Word guides responsible decision-making.

This type of integration does not occur naturally in secular social-emotional learning programs, despite the best intentions. Schools operate within constraints that limit discussions of faith, which leaves families to bridge the gap between what’s taught at school and what they believe about human flourishing.

Moving Forward with Wisdom and Discernment

Parents who want to support their teens’ emotional development while maintaining their faith must learn to navigate a balancing act. Social-emotional learning programs in schools are neither harmful nor sufficient on their own. These programs provide a piece of a larger framework that can be helpful for adolescents who struggle with basic skills, emotion recognition, and conflict resolution.

Parents must be actively involved in conversations regarding what their teens are learning and how it aligns with their family values. This requires that they ask questions about the curriculum content and understand the specific approach being used, so that gaps may be filled in at home.

Christian counselors play an essential role in this process because they can help adolescents develop emotional and social skills within a framework that honors their faith. They address the mental health challenges that social-emotional learning programs alone cannot resolve.

Teens are dealing with anxiety, depression, trauma, or other significant troubles. They benefit from professional counseling that integrates faith. Counselors trained in mental health for teens do more than teach coping strategies; they help teens understand their struggles in the context of God’s truth and provide strategies to process difficult emotions in healthy ways.

Families navigating this issue can gain wisdom by recognizing that mental health for teens requires multiple supports. Schools can teach basic emotional and social skills. Families reinforce faith-based values and provide unconditional love and support.

When churches and Christian counselors are integrated into the support system, teens can find community, spiritual guidance, and specialized care that addresses their mental health needs and honors their families’ faith.

To connect with a Christian counselor, reach out to a faith-based counseling center near you or to someone on this site. Together, we can help foster social-emotional learning that helps teens thrive.

item.title: 6 Things to Remember If Your Loved One Has ADHD
item.description:
As a neurotypical person, it can be hard to understand how people with ADHD function and why they do the things they do. Even when the diagnosis makes sense and now there is a logical explanation for their behavior, it can still be difficult to know how to connect with them.

Those with ADHD have many private struggles and experience hardships that they can’t articulate. Having some insight and understanding of the disorder will help you be patient and supportive of them in the times that they need it.

6 Things to Remember If Your Loved One Has ADHD

Their brain is literally wired differently

ADHD is classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder, which means that the nervous system and the brain have developed differently from those of neurotypical people. People with ADHD are not less intelligent, nor are they flawed; they are different. These differences are significant, however, and they tend to make life difficult for people with ADHD.

The differences in a person with ADHD’s brain ultimately affect their emotions, mood, the way they react to stimuli, the way they retain information, and even their impulse control. Besides having notably different structures from those of neurotypical people, a person with ADHD’s brain has functional differences, neurochemical differences, and network differences.

The differences are not minor. They impact your loved one’s attention span, focus, speech, ability to organize, the way they see the passing of time, and other crucial functions that you might take for granted. They are quite literally wired differently.

Understandably, you might lose your patience with them from time to time. Try to remember, though, that their forgetfulness, time blindness, disorganization, and unusual quirks are often as frustrating to them as they are to you.

If you haven’t seen much evidence of these peculiarities, it may be because they have learned to mask the majority of their unusual behavior from the public. This is a mentally and emotionally taxing instinct that many people with ADHD perform, and they do it to avoid being judged or rejected by others. The most loving thing you can do for them is to offer a safe, nonjudgmental space for them to be themselves.

Their forgetfulness isn’t personal and is probably something they are working on

It’s no secret that those with ADHD tend to be more forgetful than most people. They might frequently forget meetings, important dates, or entire conversations. When this happens, it’s easy to feel frustrated or even betrayed, but they are not being forgetful on purpose. What’s more, they are likely doing their best to be less forgetful. Give them a break and offer to help them remember important things that they would otherwise struggle with.

Forgetfulness among those with ADHD is to do with their brain structure, once again. Most people have a natural ability to control their impulses, filter their communication, remember information, and manage their time. This is called executive function.

People with ADHD have something called executive dysfunction, meaning that they do not have these abilities or can only perform them with tremendous effort. In addition to executive dysfunction, most of those with ADHD struggle with not being able to maintain regular sleep patterns. This alone can have a disastrous effect on their memory.

It’s hard for them to make simple decisions

The ability to perform simple tasks is an important part of a neurotypical brain. This includes things like making decisions.

In a single day, most people have to make countless decisions, from what to wear and eat at meals to high-stakes, demanding decisions that cannot be made in a hurry. The primary area of your brain responsible for performing these tasks is a complex zone known as the prefrontal cortex.

It begins developing in infancy and comes to maturity around twenty-five years old. It is the reason you can plan, regulate your emotions, understand complex issues, manage your attitude, and plan.

By contrast, the prefrontal cortex of a person with ADHD develops more slowly, maturing only in their late twenties or early thirties. Besides this, their prefrontal cortex is generally smaller in size and remains partially underdeveloped even later in life.

If you wonder why your loved one with ADHD seems stuck in a child-like mode, this might be the explanation. Avoid being condescending with them. Instead, have the same patience with them that you would afford a child.

They are frequently emotionally dysregulated, and that’s exhausting for them

You might have experienced emotional dysregulation at some point in your life. It is when you feel out of control of your emotions, and they feel intense and disconnected from anything particular. You might have seethed with anger as you heard your partner breathing, or burst into tears while seeing a cheesy advertisement on TV.

With neurotypicals, these mood swings are usually connected to hormones (in both men and women), outside stressors, pregnancy, menopause, or menstrual cycles. However, for many with ADHD, this is a daily experience.

Overblown emotional reactions to something minor, unpredictable emotions, or struggling to calm down from any intense emotion are common for someone with ADHD. That doesn’t mean to say it’s an easy thing to handle. It isn’t for you, and it certainly isn’t for them either.

Not everyone with ADHD will experience it to the same degree, and it might be worse at certain times, but it is one of the many struggles of living with the disorder. Work with them to help them find a way of coping with the dysregulation, and don’t give up on them.

They will procrastinate, but it might be more complex than you realize

Having a brain that doesn’t allow for easy organization or time-keeping will result in missed deadlines, rescheduled appointments, and irate bosses. We tend to judge others according to our abilities and hold them to standards we have no problem maintaining. However, most people with ADHD either can’t function in the same way as everyone else or are afraid to.

The tendency to procrastinate often comes from perfectionism and a fear of rejection. Many with ADHD are aware of their shortcomings and have been emotionally scarred by falling short all of their lives.

Perfectionism is a form of mental and emotional paralysis, and so many people with ADHD become a self-fulfilling prophecy. They want to do their best, but they focus so intently on the task that they miss the deadline, resulting in less than perfect results. This is often an extremely tender topic for those with ADHD, so proceed with caution and a lot of grace if you intend to talk with them about it.

They are trying harder than you realize

ADHD is a complicated disorder, but one thing that is universally true for someone with ADHD is that they are putting in more effort and generally trying harder than most people realize. In any field, whether academic, corporate, creative, or emotional, they are likely trying to appear as neurotypical. That’s besides the energy required of them to do their job, stay focused, regulate their emotions, and produce perfect results.

Many people with ADHD tend to be private people who make space for a handful of trusted friends in their lives. This is often because it’s easier for them to be alone or around people who understand and accept them for who they are.

Having a loved one with ADHD means having the opportunity to learn and grow in sensitivity, grace, and patience. No one wants to be condescended to, but everyone wants to know that they are worth making an effort for.

Many with ADHD are diagnosed late in life and have spent the majority of their lives struggling with simple tasks and executive dysfunction. The more you learn about the disorder, the more you can help them understand themselves. Nothing feels better than feeling seen, understood, and loved, despite the differences, or maybe because of them.

ADHD is a complex disorder that affects people to different degrees. If you would like more information or support in dealing with ADHD, we recommend meeting with a counselor. If you would like to meet with a counselor, contact us to learn about the resources available to you and your loved one.

item.title: How Do You Heal When the Past Still Hurts? Balancing Parental Regret and Reconciliation
item.description:
Parenting is often described as the most rewarding journey in life, but it’s also one of the most complicated. No parent gets it right all the time. Maybe you raised your voice more than you wanted to. Maybe you worked long hours and missed milestones. Maybe you struggled with your own challenges and didn’t have the energy to give your child the attention they needed.

Whatever the reason, regret has a way of creeping in, sometimes years later, when you look back and wish things had been different.

If you’re carrying parental regret, you’re not alone. Many parents feel this weight. The hard part is when the past still hurts, when your child remembers the pain, when you still feel guilt, and when reconciliation feels out of reach.

Yet healing is possible from the murky waters of parental regret, and with honesty, patience, and support, families can move forward, even when the past feels heavy.

Why Regret Hurts So Deeply

Regret isn’t just about wishing you had done things differently. It’s about love. You regret because you care. You regret it because you wanted the best for your child, and you feel you fell short. That’s why it hurts so much, because it touches the deepest part of your identity as a parent.

For many, regret surfaces later in life. Maybe your child is now a teenager or an adult, and they’ve started sharing how your choices affected them. Or maybe you’ve had time to reflect and realize the impact of your actions. Either way, regret can feel overwhelming, especially when the past can’t be changed.

The Impact of Cultural and Generational Expectations

One issue often overlooked in conversations about parental regrets is the role of cultural and generational expectations. Many parents grew up in environments where emotional expression was discouraged, discipline was strict, or survival took priority over nurturing. In those contexts, showing affection or listening deeply to children wasn’t always modeled or valued.

As a result, parents may look back and regret not being more emotionally available, but they also recognize they were doing the best they could with the tools they had. Children, however, may still carry hurt because their needs for warmth and understanding weren’t met. This gap between intention and impact is where reconciliation becomes so important.

Healing requires acknowledging both realities: the parent’s limitations shaped by culture and circumstance, and the child’s lived experience of feeling unseen or unheard. When parents openly share their background, explaining the pressures they faced, the lessons they were taught, and the struggles they carried, it helps children understand the context. At the same time, listening to how those choices affected the child validates their pain.

Bridging these generational differences can be powerful. It allows families to break cycles, redefine what love and connection look like, and create new traditions that prioritize emotional safety. For example, a parent who grew up in a household where “children should be seen and not heard” can intentionally create space for their own children to voice opinions, ask questions, and feel respected.

Reconciliation in this context isn’t about blaming the past – it’s about learning from it. By recognizing cultural and generational influences, parents and children can move forward with compassion, understanding, and a shared commitment to doing better together.

Why Reconciliation Matters

Reconciliation is not about erasing the past; it’s about creating a healthier future. When parents acknowledge regret and take steps toward healing, they open the door to stronger relationships. Children, whether young or grown, benefit from seeing their parents take responsibility and show vulnerability. It teaches them that mistakes can be repaired and that love can grow even after conflict.

For parents, reconciliation brings relief. It eases guilt, reduces emotional distance, and restores a sense of connection. It’s a chance to move forward with peace instead of carrying the weight of unresolved pain.

Common Barriers to Healing

Even when parents want reconciliation, obstacles can get in the way:

Fear of rejection: You worry your child won’t forgive you.

Pride: Admitting mistakes feels uncomfortable.

Unresolved hurt: Your child may still feel angry or distant.

Timing: You hope the issue will fade, but silence often makes the gap wider.

Recognizing these barriers is the first step to overcoming them. Healing requires courage, humility, and persistence.

Real-Life Times of Regret and Healing

Picture that father who worked long hours remembers missing his daughter’s school plays. Years later, she tells him how much it hurt. Instead of defending himself, he apologizes and asks how he can be more present now. They begin a new tradition of weekly dinners, creating memories that heal old wounds.

Or a mother who recalls yelling during stressful times. Her son, now grown, admits he still feels the sting of those words. She listens, acknowledges the pain, and expresses regret. Over time, their conversations become more open, and trust begins to rebuild.

These examples show that reconciliation doesn’t require perfection. It requires honesty, effort, and a willingness to change.

Practical Steps Toward Healing

Here are steps you can take if you’re ready to move forward:

Acknowledge the regret: Be honest with yourself about what you wish had been different.

Express it openly: Share your feelings with your child, without excuses.

Listen deeply: Allow your child to express their perspective, even if it’s painful.

Apologize sincerely: A genuine apology can open doors to healing.

Make changes: Show through actions that you are committed to doing better.

Be patient: Rebuilding trust takes time.

Seek support: Family counseling can provide guidance and a safe space for reconciliation.

When the Past Still Hurts

Sometimes, even after apologies, the past continues to hurt. Your child may not be ready to forgive. You may still feel guilt. Healing in these moments requires patience and persistence.

  • Give space and allow your child time to process.
  • Stay consistent and show through actions that you’re committed to change.
  • Work on yourself and address your own guilt and pain with counseling or support groups.
  • Keep communication open. Even small gestures of care can help rebuild trust.

Healing doesn’t happen overnight. It’s a journey, and every step matters.

Family counseling offers tools that help parents and children communicate more effectively. A counselor provides a neutral space where both sides feel heard. They can guide conversations, help manage emotions, and suggest practical strategies for rebuilding trust. Counseling is not about assigning blame; it’s about creating pathways to understanding and connection.

Reconciliation doesn’t always come from grand gestures. Small, consistent changes often make the biggest difference. A parent who starts checking in daily, offering encouragement, or showing up for small moments demonstrates commitment. Over time, these actions rebuild trust and show children that regret has turned into growth.

If you’re reading this and feeling the sting of regret, pause for a moment. Think about the relationship you want with your child today, not the one you had years ago, but the one you can build now. Regret means you care. It means you’re aware. And awareness is the first step toward change.

Your child doesn’t need you to be perfect. They need you to be present, honest, and willing to grow. Even if they’re older now – even if they have families of their own, it’s never too late to reach out. A phone call, a heartfelt conversation, or even a simple “I’m sorry” can open doors you thought were closed forever.

Turning Regret into Growth

Parental regret doesn’t have to remain a source of pain. It can become a catalyst for growth. By facing regret honestly, you model resilience and humility. You show your child that relationships can heal, even after mistakes. Families discover that reconciliation brings not only peace but also deeper love.

If you are a parent carrying regret and longing for reconciliation, don’t wait. Healing is possible, and support is available.

Reach out today; call the numbers on this site to speak to a representative. They will connect you with family counselors who can guide you through the process of reconciliation. Together, you can turn regret into renewal and build stronger, healthier bonds with your children.

item.title: Becoming a Healthy Parent for Your Kids When a Borderline Mother Raised You
item.description:
Many people hear the term borderline personality, and they think of something distant or a diagnosis that belongs to someone else’s story. Yet, for those raised by a mother who struggled with emotional swings and fear of rejection, it’s part of your story. It shaped how you learned to love, how you handled conflict, and how you saw yourself.

It’s a lived experience. It was the reality you expected every day.

You learned to read her moods before you learned to trust your own. You may have felt responsible for keeping her calm or happy, even when you were just a child. Understanding this helps you see that your borderline mother’s behavior wasn’t about your worth; it was about her pain.

Now, as a parent, you’re trying to create something different. A home grounded in peace and emotional safety. This article will help you understand what shaped you and how you can get help to raise children who feel stable and secure with healthier parenting.

Familiar Patterns You Might Remember from Childhood

Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a complex mental health condition marked by intense emotional instability, fear of abandonment, and difficulty maintaining consistent relationships. When a mother lives with BPD, these traits can deeply affect her parenting style and her children’s emotional development.

A borderline mother tends to feel emotions deeply and react quickly. Her love can feel intense one day and distant the next. She may crave closeness but fear rejection, which makes relationships confusing and unstable.

If you were raised by a borderline mother, you probably remember certain patterns that shaped how you view love and safety.

Emotional unpredictability: Impulsivity, unstable self-image, and intense but short-lived relationships.

Emotional swings: A borderline mother may swing rapidly between affection and anger, leaving children uncertain about safety and love.

Fear of rejection: This can lead to clinginess or controlling behavior toward children, as the mother seeks reassurance through them.

Identity confusion: Her sense of self may depend on others’ approval, making parenting decisions inconsistent or reactive.

Such behavior does leave deep marks on a child. They taught you to walk carefully, to please others, and to avoid conflict. They also make it hard to relax into love as an adult, especially when you’re raising your own children.

Why Consistency and Safety are so Hard for a Borderline Mother to Maintain

Consistency requires emotional steadiness, and that’s something a borderline mother struggles to hold. Her emotions can swing from warmth to rejection in minutes. When she feels abandoned or misunderstood, she reacts from fear, not reason.

This instability affects parenting because children need predictability to feel safe. When love feels conditional, they learn to perform for approval instead of trusting they’re loved for who they are. A borderline mother doesn’t mean to create this confusion; she’s reacting to her own inner chaos.

Still, the result is a home where kids don’t feel free, and affection feels uncertain.

If you grew up in that kind of environment, you may still carry the belief that love must be earned or that peace is temporary. Recognizing this is the first step toward changing how you parent now.

Recognizing the Patterns You Inherited Without Realizing It

Even when you promise yourself you’ll parent differently, old habits can sneak in. You may find yourself subconsciously reacting sharply when your child cries or withdrawing when you feel criticized. These reactions aren’t random; they’re learned responses from years of emotional survival.

You might notice that you:

  • Struggle to stay calm when your child’s emotions feel overwhelming.
  • Feel guilty for setting boundaries.
  • Overcompensate by trying to be the perfect parent.
  • Avoid conflict because it reminds you of childhood tension.

This is because you learned to protect yourself in ways that made sense at the time. Now, you have to start learning to unlearn them, not through shame, but through awareness.

Growing Up Confused About Love, Boundaries, and Self-Worth

When love was unpredictable, boundaries felt unsafe. You may have learned that saying “no” led to anger or rejection. As an adult, that confusion can spill into your parenting. You might struggle to balance kindness with firmness or feel guilty for disciplining your child.

Children of borderline mothers often grow up believing their feelings are too much or not enough. That belief can make it hard to trust your instincts as a parent. You may question whether you’re being too strict or too lenient, too emotional or too detached.

But healthy parenting isn’t about perfection; it’s about presence. It’s about learning to stay steady even when emotions rise. It’s about teaching your children that love doesn’t disappear when someone makes a mistake.

A healthy home doesn’t mean a flawless one. It means a place where love feels safe, not earned. You can start building that kind of environment by focusing on small, consistent actions that teach your children what stability should be like.

Breaking the cycle isn’t a one-time decision, but should become a daily practice. That means choosing awareness over reaction and grace over guilt.

Daily Steps to Break the Emotional Cycle Every Day

Teach your child to check the temperature: Instead of asking, “What’s wrong?” when emotions rise, teach them to notice what’s happening inside. “How are you feeling right now?” It helps them name feelings without shame and reminds you to do the same. It turns emotional awareness into a shared language instead of a power struggle.

Come up with a reset ritual: When tension builds, have a simple family reset. Maybe everyone takes a short walk, drinks water, or sits quietly for two minutes. It’s not punishment; it’s a way to remind your child that calm is always possible. It also teaches them that peace is something you practice, not something that just appears.

Use truth moments instead of lectures: When your child misbehaves, skip long explanations. Say one honest sentence that connects emotion and consequence: “I get frustrated too, but yelling doesn’t fix it.” It models accountability without shame and shows that emotions can be handled with honesty instead of fear.

Let your child see you recenter: If you lose your temper, don’t just apologize; explain what you’re doing to make it right. Say, “I was angry, and I’m working on calming down before I speak.” It teaches emotional responsibility and shows that repair is part of love, not a sign of weakness.

Build safe silence: Children of emotionally unpredictable parents often fear silence because it means rejection. Encourage times of comfortable silence that feel safe, like reading together, sitting in the car, or praying before bed. It helps them learn that silence can mean peace, not punishment.

Practice emotion swaps: When your child expresses frustration, respond with curiosity instead of control. Ask, “What would help you feel better right now?” It teaches problem-solving and emotional flexibility, skills you may never have seen modeled growing up.

Keep a compassion list: Write down a few ways you’ve shown patience or kindness each week. Share one with your child: “I was proud of how we handled that argument.” It reinforces progress and teaches gratitude without turning it into a performance.

End the day with emotional check-ins: Before bedtime, ask, “Was there anything today that felt unfair or confusing?” It gives your child permission to speak honestly and helps you catch patterns early. It also models emotional reflection, something many adults raised by borderline mothers never learned.

Healing doesn’t mean forgetting your past. It means learning from it without letting it define your future. If a borderline mother raised you, you’ve already done something brave; you’ve started asking how to parent differently. That question alone shows growth. You’re not doomed to repeat the same patterns. Through awareness, faith, and professional support, you can create a home where love feels steady and safe.

If this topic speaks to you, consider reaching out for professional counseling. A family therapist can help you understand your history, strengthen your emotional foundation, and guide you toward healthier parenting. Talk to a professional listed on this site or call the numbers on the screen to take that next step toward healing and peace.

item.title: Why Am I So Angry All the Time? Practical Tips to Overcome Anger
item.description:
The Heart Angle

It is important to discuss anger from a heartfelt perspective, although anger is not known for being a heartfelt emotion. When a person asks why they are so angry all the time, the root cause may not be known, so the question will only be partially answered.

The root cause for a great deal of the anger that is experienced derives from issues or matters of the heart. There is a saying that says there is a thin line between love and hate. Indeed, it is so thin that at times their distance from one another is small.

As a therapist, I have found that when anger is unpacked, it often stems from heartbreak caused by disappointment, loss, grief, lack of progress, feelings of failure, rejection, abandonment, and even a lack of felt love. Anger is often telling you what you are avoiding.

Emotions are the byproduct of the deeper symptoms. What is going on in your heart that is portraying itself as anger? To answer this question, we must go underneath. Your anger is trying to tell you something. The question is: what? This is often what is occurring.

  • There is hurt without clarity.
  • Undealt-with rejection.
  • Unhealed abandonment.
  • You may be feeling powerless.
  • You may be feeling ignored.
  • You may have tolerated something for too long.
  • You may be feeling stuck.
  • You may even be angry because there is a truth somewhere in your life that you have been unwilling or unable to confront.

Take the time to consider each thought. Allow it to sit with you.

Anger and Our Relationship with the Truth

I believe a great deal of anger can be connected to our relationship with truth. Sometimes we are angry because we cannot tell the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we do not want to face the truth. Sometimes we are angry because we are not living according to what we know is true.

Then there are times when we are angry because someone else told us the truth and we were not ready to hear it. The truth can be uncomfortable. Truth can seem threatening. Truth can even seem insulting without the intention of being so.

Maybe you continue saying yes to people when you really want to push back. Yet the deeper problem may not be that people keep asking. The deeper problem may be that you have not been honest about what you can handle. You have trouble admitting your limitations, and you would rather die than have anyone perceive a weakness.

Perhaps you are angry about your lack of professional progression. You are feeling overlooked by your superiors and undervalued. You resent your coworkers for getting what you deserve. You used to love your company and once saw a future there. But now you dread work mornings. Deep down, you know it is time to make a change, but fear has prevented you from making a change.

Truth will also require you to acknowledge when you have participated in your own frustration. There are times when we remain in situations long after we know something must change. Nevertheless, we become angry with people for crossing boundaries we have never verbalized or enforced.

We may even become irritated when others do not recognize needs that we have never expressed. Standing toe to toe with truth means asking yourself what part of the situation belongs to you. That moment may be uncomfortable, but it can help show us where we still have the power to move differently.

Your anger is real. But so is the hurtful and hard-to-face truth underneath it. Jesus said that the truth would make us free. Freedom has never begun with pretending. Freedom requires us to become willing to see what is there. Sometimes anger increases because we are fighting reality that we feel helpless to change.

Think About It, You May Not Be Angry About Today

A major reason why anger can feel disproportionate is that the current situation is carrying the weight of several previous situations. Someone does something tiny, and in return you respond enormously. Ever wonder when you became so upset? The other person may wonder the same thing.

The answer could be that you were not only responding to what happened today, because that is all you can see in the moment. However, you neglected to really comprehend that you were responding to every time you felt overlooked. Not to mention every time you were disappointed, or for each time a promise was broken, or for each conversation that went unresolved.

Think about it, you may not be angry about today, but for every moment you have decided not to say anything. Your anger had been accumulating when experiences that you had in your life were not properly processed. This is why it is not unusual to encounter some people going from zero to one hundred over something that appears insignificant.

The current situation may simply be the final place where everything else came to a head. In those intense moments, ask yourself, “What else am I responding to right now?” The answer could separate today’s frustration from yesterday’s wound.

Practical Tips to Overcome Anger

The goal of overcoming anger is not to become a person who never gets angry. This is unrealistic and not maintainable. The key to overcoming anger is learning how to recognize what your anger is revealing before it begins attempting to take center stage. Your anger becomes more manageable when you have practical steps that can help you move from reacting to your anger toward understanding it and responding differently.

Identify what is happening beneath the anger Instead of “I am upset,” finish the sentence: “I am angry because I felt…” Permit yourself to go above and beyond what may have been your obvious answer. Were you feeling ashamed? Did you feel disregarded? Did you feel powerless? Remember, naming what is at the root of your anger will aid you in understanding what really needs your attention,

Start separating what you can change from what you cannot control Ask: “What am I avoiding?” You may already know what needs to be changed. The hard part may be accepting what that truth may require from us.

Do not shut down speaking what you feel sooner Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. You cannot control another person’s choices. You can control what you participate in. You can decide what you will tolerate. You can also determine what access someone will continue to have to you.

Examine your expectations Determine what was conveyed. Do not make silence carry something until anger has to announce it. Learn to communicate frustration while it is still frustration. Not everything requires confrontation, but important matters should not continually be buried.

Decide what you should be grieving instead of correcting Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. Some things cannot be fixed. They must be mourned. You may be trying to get an apology you will never receive or attempting to change something that has already happened. Grief may be necessary where correction is no longer possible.

Choose what your anger will yield Let it lead to a boundary, conversation, decision, healing work, or change rather than damage. Anger has energy attached to it. Decide where that energy will go. Your anger can destroy something or reveal what needs to be different. The responsibility is deciding what happens next.

item.title: What BPD in Women Looks Like
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder is a condition born from complex childhood trauma. A person with BPD experiences crippling loneliness, fear of abandonment, anger control issues, struggles with identity and self-worth, and usually has a history of unstable relationships and broken friendships.

It is not something you were born with; it is the result of complex trauma that you went through when you were too young to process your emotions. While it is still diagnosed the same, BPD in women comes with its own set of unique challenges and experiences. The distinction is important because sometimes the first step in recovery from BPD is to have your particular struggles seen and your unique experiences validated.

The Stigma of BPD

Low self-esteem and self-image issues are among the core effects of BPD, which obviously contribute to the struggle. Besides having to deal with issues like these, people with BPD regularly carry shame surrounding their diagnosis, feeling as if they are too dramatic, too complicated, or broken beyond repair.

These feelings are often confirmed by the way other people treat them. From the outside, people see things like anger issues, impulsive and unpredictable behavior, and many damaged relationships, and cast blame. Being seen as the villain does not help someone who has a crippling fear of abandonment in every relationship they develop.

Besides this, people sometimes dismiss BPD as “attention-seeking behavior”, a bad attitude, or a toxic personality. BPD in women is a magnified issue because historically, women have been labeled as overly emotional, impulsive, or melodramatic.

The truth is that people with BPD were neglected at a vulnerable and critical phase of their development, with too many complex emotions and experiences to process. They are not too much; they simply had too much to deal with at too young an age.

Is BPD in women different?

While the diagnostic criteria for determining BPD do not change for women, and gender does not always affect the way BPD looks, certain critical aspects make BPD in women a unique experience. As with any mental health condition, the way it presents can look different depending on the individual, their age, their background, and a host of other things. It is the same condition, but it is sometimes displayed through different lenses.

At a certain age, emotional dysregulation becomes part of the monthly experience for many women. BPD in women generally means having to face more acute emotional instability, though. These are not the mood swings associated with hormones, either. With BPD, there are more intense emotions that shift rapidly and unpredictably and feel impossible to control.

All people with BPD experience bouts of emptiness and depression, but research shows that this is a more chronic issue for women with BPD. They tend to become suicidal more often than men and develop self-harming tendencies in most cases.

There are also unique combinations of disorders that women with BPD have to deal with that affect men less frequently. For example, it is common for BPD in women to exist alongside anxiety, eating disorders, and PTSD, while men more commonly tend to experience antisocial traits and substance abuse with BPD.

Without an official diagnosis for BPD, any one of the unique traits associated with the disorder could steal focus. A woman might believe she is depressed to the point of feeling suicidal, while also struggling in relationships and missing the fact that it is BPD causing each of these issues. One person’s experience with BPD might be different from someone else’s, even when they have a similar history and personality.

What BPD in Women Looks Like in Relationships

Relationships are the area that gives more clues to a person’s mental health struggles than anywhere else, particularly with BPD. Men and women tend to navigate friendships, romantic partnerships, and intimacy differently from each other, and with BPD, these differences can become a little more pronounced. On the other hand, BPD causes people to be unpredictable and emotionally unstable, regardless of their gender.

People with BPD will send intense mixed signals, from being almost obsessed with someone for a while before becoming disinterested in a short time. They might go from dismissing their partner’s needs and ignoring their preferences one day, to expressing their unfaltering devotion to the relationship the next.

These kinds of mood swings are often unfairly attributed to women in general, but these levels of unpredictable, toxic behavior often point to an underlying condition, whether in men or women.

For people with BPD, relationships and friendships will always be chaotic and complicated. They have the tendency to elevate certain people, romantic or otherwise, to a god-like status, before completely devaluing them without warning.

BPD brings with it more arguments, disagreements, and falling-outs than the average adult friend circle. When a person’s friendships and family connections are constantly fraught with drama and intensity, it should count as a warning sign pointing to a mental health struggle.

Statistically, fewer women are shown to have anger control issues with BPD than men. This does not mean that BPD in women does not cause anger or rage issues. People with BPD regularly respond with anger that is disproportionate to the situation.

Culturally, it might be more expected to see men in a towering rage over certain things because anger presents as a masculine emotion. Uncontrollable anger, however, often points to emotional regulation issues, especially when it doesn’t match the trigger.

Many people struggle with identity issues, confidence, and shifting goals; it’s part of growing up and finding your feet in life. People with BPD consistently struggle with their identity, and this affects everything, from their career goals to their relationships. They might be focused on a goal or a life plan for months, only to unexpectedly drop it and change directions.

From the outside, it looks like they are being inexplicably erratic, while inside, they are dealing with low self-confidence and fear of abandonment should they not meet their goal. A fear of being abandoned by others underpins almost every major decision in a person’s life when they are dealing with BPD.

BPD in women also regularly shows up in the impulsive way she handles her finances, in her constantly changing appearance, and in her hobbies and interests, particularly if they are constantly changing.

Each of these things will inevitably affect her relationships and close friendships, whether she is aware of it or not. Without knowing anything about BPD, she might be labeled as immature, impulsive, or toxic, when in truth she is dealing with something more difficult than others could ever realize.

Recovery From BPD in Women

Dealing with BPD is not a life sentence, and many people recover to the point that they no longer meet the criteria for diagnosis when retested. It is not an infectious disease that can be healed, but it is also not a condition someone is born with; it is a result of complex trauma that can be treated and resolved.

Women with BPD have to face struggles like stigma, stereotypes, misdiagnoses, gendered blame, and the systemic invalidation of their struggles, all as she deals with extreme emotions, low self-esteem, and a fear of abandonment. It could take years of employing evidence-based therapies, but it is possible to recover fully from BPD and have a life of unproblematic relationships and a secure attachment.

You are not alone as you deal with BPD. If you would like to research your options for therapy and support, we can help. We host an online catalog of counselors that we would love you to explore. We hope you find someone suitable to meet with. If you would rather speak with someone who can help you find a counselor, our reception team will be happy to help.

item.title: Anxiety Disorders: What They Are and What to Do
item.description:
What is anxiety?

We’ve all felt anxious about something. Adrenaline rushes in. Cortisol gives us that unmistakable sense of dread. Our heart races. Breathing becomes shallow. We tense up and sweat buckets, our head pounds, and our stomach aches.

While not a pleasant experience, anxiety can be a normal human response to stressors in our environment. Normal anxiety is a temporary and realistic response to pressures such as taking a test or interviewing for a job. Once the event is over, the anxiety resolves.

Anxiety is a God-given reaction meant to protect us from dangerous situations. When we feel unsafe, our body responds with one of four mechanisms: fight, flight, freeze, and fawn. Most of us are familiar with the first three. The fourth is a learned trauma response “where a person finds themselves responding to someone they perceive as dangerous by engaging in people-pleasing and submissive behaviors” (Fawning Trauma Response: Why It Happens & How to Stop, 2024).

These four responses in themselves do not signal that a person has an anxiety disorder. They are usually brief, resolve in minutes, and are triggered in proportionate response to our environment. So, when exactly does anxiety meet the criteria?

Diagnostic Manual Definition of Anxiety Disorders

Anxiety disorders, according to the DSM-5-TR, the American Psychiatric Association’s diagnostic manual, are “disorders that share features of excessive fear and anxiety… Anxiety disorders differ from developmentally normative fear or anxiety by being excessive or persisting beyond developmentally appropriate periods…typically lasting 6 months or more” (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

Consequently, the level and duration of fear and anxiety are key factors in what comprises a disorder. For example, two weeks spent stressing over an interview is normal. Suffering months of debilitating dread about the idea of being interviewed, and then sabotaging future employment opportunities because of it, is not.

Jesus tells us in Matt. 6:34 to avoid spending our life in chronic anxiety. He instructs us instead to deal with each day’s troubles as they come and not worry about troubles that haven’t yet taken place. He wasn’t just giving us a set of rules. Jesus knew that chronic worry leads to great harm if left unchecked.

Harmful Impacts of Chronic Anxiety

Healthline online breaks down the different impacts that long-term exposure to high stress has on the body. Physically, it can lead to excessive weight gain or loss. Cardiovascular issues could also arise, such as high blood pressure and heart disease, which increase the risk of coronary events such as heart attacks.

Other problems include digestive issues such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or chronic infections. Those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) “may be at an increased risk of hospitalization from anxiety-related complications” (Cherney, 2022). Muscle tension, depression, and isolation from social activities compound the issue.

Neurologically, the impacts of chronic stress are just as damaging. Stress triggers the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. This is the primary pathway that kicks in the fight, flight, freeze, and fawn reflexes. When the HPA is activated for too long, this can cause:

  • Hormonal imbalances that affect mood and cognition
  • Neurochemical disruptions that interfere with serotonin and dopamine (key players in emotional regulation)
  • Overstimulation of the amygdala, making you more anxious or reactive
  • Damage to the hippocampus, which is vital for memory and learning
  • Reduced function in the prefrontal cortex, impairing focus, planning, and decision-making (The Connection Between Stress and Neurological Disorders, 2025).

When fight, flight, freeze, and fawn remain in overdrive, the autonomic nervous system never allows for the “parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) system that helps you recover” (Ibid). The brain needs this permission to rest and digest. Without it, lasting changes occur in the structure and function of the brain, which can lead to depression and/or anxiety disorders from an overstimulated amygdala (Ibid).

Types of Anxiety Disorders

Now that we have an idea of how anxiety affects the body and brain, let’s take a closer look at the actual disorders and their diagnostic criteria. Please note that this is a general overview of each disorder. It is not meant to be used for personal diagnosis. If you believe you or someone you know might have an anxiety disorder, please reach out to a licensed mental health professional for help.

The following are general overviews from the DSM-5-TR:

Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Diagnostic Criteria

Includes excessive anxiety about events or activities (such as work or school performance). Signs and symptoms are:

  • Restlessness
  • Getting tired easily
  • Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank
  • Irritability
  • Muscle tension
  • Poor sleep

Panic Disorder

Includes recurrent unexpected panic attacks. Symptoms of a panic attack include:

  • Palpitations, pounding heart, or accelerated heart rate
  • Sweating
  • Trembling or shaking
  • Sensations of shortness of breath or smothering
  • Feelings of choking
  • Chest pain or discomfort
  • Nausea or abdominal distress
  • Feeling dizzy, unsteady, light-headed, or faint
  • Chills or heat sensations
  • Paresthesia (numbness or tingling sensations)
  • Derealization (feelings of unreality) or depersonalization (being detached from oneself)
  • Fear of losing control or “going crazy”
  • Fear of dying

Agoraphobia

Includes excessive anxiety about two (or more) of the following five situations:

  • Using public transportation
  • Being in open spaces
  • Being in enclosed places
  • Standing in line or being in a crowd
  • Being outside of the home alone

Social Anxiety Disorder

Includes excessive anxiety about social situations. (Some examples: having a conversation, meeting a stranger, being observed eating or drinking, performing in front of others – e.g., giving a speech). The person fears negative evaluation, such as being humiliated or embarrassed, and being rejected by or offending others.

Specific Phobias

Includes excessive anxiety about a specific object or situation (e.g., flying, heights, animals, receiving an injection, seeing blood). The phobic object or situation provokes anxiety that is out of proportion to the actual danger posed by the specific object or situation.

Separation Anxiety in Adults

Includes developmentally inappropriate and excessive anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures. The individual may show:

  • Excessive distress about being separated from home or from major attachment figures.
  • Excessive worry about losing major attachment figures or about possible harm to them, such as illness, injury, disasters, or death.
  • Excessive worry about experiencing an untoward event (e.g., getting lost, being kidnapped, having an accident, becoming ill) that causes separation from a major attachment figure.
  • Reluctance or refusal to go out, away from home, to school, to work, or elsewhere because of fear of separation.
  • Excessive fear of or reluctance about being alone or without major attachment figures at home or in other settings.
  • Reluctance or refusal to sleep away from home or to go to sleep without being near a major attachment figure.
  • Repeated nightmares involving the theme of separation.
  • Repeated complaints of physical symptoms when separation from major attachment figures occurs or is anticipated.

The fear, anxiety, or avoidance is persistent, lasting at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents and typically 6 months or more in adults (Ibid).

OCD and PTSD

While OCD and PTSD are not classified as anxiety disorders, they do share overlapping mechanisms, including excessive fear or anxiety that significantly impact vocational and social functioning. It’s important to get help with these or any of the other disorders on the list, as they significantly affect daily functioning.

How Anxiety Manifests in Daily Life

Anxiety disorders negatively influence relational, educational, or vocational functioning. While acute stress might cause occasional disruption such as missing a day of work, chronic stress from an anxiety disorder has a much more outsized impact. Some of these impacts include:

Workplace – Procrastination, over-preparation, avoidance of meetings, burnout, loss of employment.

Relationships – Reassurance seeking, people-pleasing behaviors, conflict avoidance, explosive confrontations, emotional withdrawal.

Parenting – Hypervigilance, overprotection, difficulty tolerating child distress, or dissociation.

Decision-making – Rumination, fear of mistakes, avoidance behaviors, sticking with what is safe.

Treatments

These impacts can seem overwhelming. It may seem as if nothing can be done to resolve the never-ending cycle of dread that comes with having an anxiety disorder. But the following therapies from qualified mental health professionals are effective treatments:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): A licensed therapist trained in CBT helps clients identify, understand, and modify their anxiety-related thought and behavior patterns through regular sessions.

Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT): DBT incorporates the philosophical practice of dialectics, in which multiple or even contradictory ideas are examined, combining acceptance and change at the same time.

Exposure therapy: A form of therapy involving gradually exposing the individual to feared situations in a safe and controlled environment, with the ultimate aim of reducing the associated anxiety.

Group therapy: Refers to therapeutic settings that involve multiple participants in addition to a single healthcare provider (Anxiety.org, 2016).

Somatic Therapies: Somatically based therapies such as EMDR, IFS, or Lifespan Integration help individuals to integrate sources of trauma that may have triggered the initial disorder.

SSRIs, SNRIs, and Other Medications: While not therapies, antidepressants have been proven to be effective treatments.

Techniques for Managing Anxiety:

It’s good to note that we can also improve our anxiety prognosis through managing our own behaviors, emotions, and thoughts. This can be seen with techniques such as:

  • Mindfulness exercises and deep breathing exercises, prayer, or meditation.
  • Physical activities such as running, walking, yoga, cycling, etc.
  • Practicing good nutrition and limiting sugar, alcohol, and caffeine (The Connection Between Stress and Neurological Disorders, 2025).

Conclusion

Anxiety disorders are common and impact millions of people every day. With proper diagnosis, therapy, and techniques, anxiety can be treated. God desires our wholeness. As the Bible says:

…for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control. – 2 Timothy 1:7 ESV
